opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so the starting point is that when a language model trains on a large corpus, there are two kinds of things it can pick up. There's knowledge that's shared across many documents, like general facts, language structure, and reasoning patterns. And there's information that's specific to one document, like a particular person's phone number, a rare string, or details that only show up once or a handful of times. In a standard model both kinds get stored in the same parameters, all entangled. That's a big part of why unlearning or removing memorized content after the fact is so hard: when you try to remove the specific stuff, you end up damaging the general capabilities, because they live in the same place.

The idea with memorization sinks is to give the model a designated place to put the document-specific information during training. Concretely, you set aside a set of units, think of them as extra neurons in the MLP layers, and each document is associated with a particular subset of those sink neurons, which you can determine from something like a document identifier. Whenever the model sees that document, those specific sink neurons are active, alongside the shared neurons that are active for everything.

Now think about the training dynamics. The shared neurons see gradients from every document, so they're pushed toward learning things that help across the whole corpus, the generalizable patterns. The sink neurons for a given document only fire when that document appears, so they're a natural place for the model to stash whatever is unique to that document and doesn't help elsewhere. You're not forcing the separation explicitly; you're setting up the architecture so that the path of least resistance for memorizing something idiosyncratic is the sink, rather than overwriting shared capacity.

Then at test time, or when you want to remove memorized content, you can just drop the sink neurons. Because the document-specific information has been channeled there, you get a model that keeps its general capabilities but has much less of the verbatim memorization. That's the nice property: the separation happens by design during training, so you're not trying to surgically untangle things afterward.

It also sheds light on a broader point I care about. Memorization isn't just a bug to suppress. Models do need to memorize some things to learn well, especially from long-tail data. So rather than fighting memorization with heavy regularization, which can hurt generalization, you give it somewhere to go. You get the learning benefit during training while keeping control over what ends up baked into the model you actually deploy.

There are still open questions. How well does this hold up at scale? How do you handle information that's repeated across a few documents, so it's somewhere between "specific" and "shared"? And how should you assign sink neurons in messy real-world data where document boundaries aren't clean? But I think the core principle, shaping where information gets stored through the training setup itself, is a promising direction for privacy, copyright, and unlearning.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so the basic idea comes from a pretty simple observation about how these models learn. When you train a language model on a big corpus, there's really two kinds of information it's absorbing at the same time. There's the general stuff, the knowledge that shows up across many documents, the facts, the patterns of language, how the world works. And then there's the document-specific stuff, the idiosyncratic details of a particular document, the exact phrasing, the particular names or numbers that appear in only that one place. And the problem is that standard training doesn't distinguish between them. The model just has one set of parameters, and it's trying to minimize loss on everything, so memorizing the idiosyncratic details of a single document ends up getting entangled with the general knowledge in the very same weights.

So the idea with memorization sinks is to give the model a place to put that document-specific information that is separate from the shared parameters. Concretely, you associate each document with its own small set of parameters, you can think of them as document-specific neurons or a little adapter that's only active when you're training on that document. During training, when the model sees a document, it has access to both the shared weights and these document-specific sink parameters. And the key dynamic is that anything that generalizes, anything that's useful across many documents, gets reinforced in the shared weights because that's the thing that's consistently helping on lots of examples. Whereas the stuff that's only useful for this one document, the model has an easier path to just stash it in the sink, because that's the cheapest way to reduce the loss on that particular sequence without disturbing anything else.

What's nice about this is that it's not forcing a hard separation through some explicit rule. It's more that you're changing the optimization landscape so that the natural gradient descent dynamics sort the information. Shared knowledge wants to live where it's shared, and memorization wants to live where it's cheap and isolated. And then at test time, or when you decide you need to remove a document, you can just drop its sink. Because the general knowledge was never really dependent on it, you don't get the catastrophic degradation you see with a lot of unlearning methods, where you try to scrub one document and you end up damaging the model's broader capabilities.

I'd say the caveat is that the separation isn't perfect. There's always some leakage, some document-specific details that end up partially in the shared weights, and some general knowledge that gets redundantly stored in the sinks. But even an imperfect separation gives you a much better handle on the problem than you had before, where everything was just one undifferentiated blob of parameters.

r003.rationale: It explains that information useful across many documents is reinforced in shared weights, while document-specific information is stored in the sink.

astra-6.text:
The intuition is to give the model a separate place to put information that’s specific to an individual document. Usually, everything has to go into the shared model parameters—both patterns that recur across documents and details that are only useful for predicting one particular document.

A memorization sink would provide a document-specific capacity for those details. If something is shared across many documents, learning it in the shared parameters helps on all of them. If it’s an arbitrary detail that only matters for one document, the sink can absorb it instead.

The tricky part is that this isn’t automatically a clean separation. The model could put useful knowledge into the sink, or still memorize details in its shared parameters. So the capacity of the sink and how you train it matter. You’d want to check whether the shared model still generalizes when that document-specific capacity isn’t available.

sol-6.1.text:
The intuition is that some information helps you predict lots of documents, while other information is useful only for predicting this particular document. If we give the model a place to store that document-specific information—a memorization sink—then it has less reason to put it into the parameters that are shared across all documents.

For example, a general pattern in language is useful everywhere, so there’s pressure to learn it in the shared parameters. An arbitrary detail that occurs in only one document could instead be captured by the sink associated with that document.

But that separation isn’t automatic. The capacity of the sink and how you train the model matter. If the sink can store everything, the model might have little incentive to learn shared structure. So the interesting question is whether you can create the right pressure for reusable knowledge to go into the shared model and document-specific details to go into the sink.
